angle: The famous infinite is real, certified twice, and shows up in 6.4% of games — so this issue is about the other 93.6%: a payoff-first Dragon board that kills on critical mass, held back by 34 lands and a land drop that becomes a coin flip on turn six.

cover.kicker: AND IT SHOWS UP IN 6.4% OF GAMES
teases: Old Gnawbone + Aggravated Assault: net +2 Treasures a cycle, two opponents dead on combats 6 and 12 (stack 006)
REFUTED: Sneak Attack cannot cheat your own commander — the command zone is not your hand (stack 005)
The spells-only trap: five of your own mana sources can never pay the combo

departments.headline: THE DRAGON YOU NEVER CAST
departments.dek: The card on the cover costs nine mana and mostly never arrives. This is an issue about what the deck does in the meantime, and about the one enchantment that decides whether the table comes for you first.

in_this_issue.line: Six lines went to the checker. One came back refuted, and it is the one your whole table believes.
Thirty-four lands, five colours, 101 coloured pips. Ledger reads the bill out loud.
Seventy-six painters across ninety-five cards. Nobody owns this deck, and that turned out to be the story.

departments.note: Margot Stet's letter is already written; this is the packaging around it. The letter opens on the nine-mana commander, so the letterhead card is deliberately NOT him — the cover is already a full-bleed Ur-Dragon and the letter's other subject, the one enchantment the whole table can name on sight, has no picture anywhere else in Act I. The three teases skip the Pilot's Log, which the letter previews itself.

departments.headline: HE BILLS FROM THE ZONE
departments.dek: Most commanders have to resolve before they matter. Yours charges the table from the command zone all game — and the record says the discount, the tax and the rental clause all argue for casting him rarely.
departments.body:
Start with what the zone guarantees: your commander is always available to cast from it (CR 903.4). No other format promises you a specific card every game. This deck files that promise differently from every other seat at the table, because The Ur-Dragon's eminence works while he sits in the zone — every other Dragon spell you cast costs {1} less, from your first upkeep, whether or not he ever moves. The guarantee is not that you will draw him. It is that you are already being paid.

Now the tax. Each cast from the zone after the first costs an additional {2} (CR 903.8), so the ladder reads nine, then eleven, then thirteen. Set that against the ledger: mean available mana is 6.165 on turn nine, and in 8,634 of 10,000 simulated games he never lands inside ten turns at all. The first cast is an event, the second is a stretch, the third is fiction. So protect the one you get. Deflecting Swat and Flawless Maneuver are free only while a commander is on your battlefield, which means keeping him beats recasting him by a distance.

There is a rental clause, and the Counselor commends it to your attention. Hellkite Courser's enters-trigger puts The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield from the command zone, hasty, for exactly one attack — a card per attacking Dragon plus a free permanent — then returns him at end step. The tax counts casts, and this never was one: the zone gets its tenant back untaxed. The route everyone assumes works does not. Sneak Attack reaches a creature card in your hand, and the command zone is not your hand (CR 903.6; the full holding is case A-005).

Colour identity costs you nothing in exclusions and everything in logistics. Five colours means no card in the format is outside your identity. It also means 34 lands answering 101 coloured pips, sixteen of which have 'enters tapped' printed somewhere on the card. Sources Say prices that bill in full. Learn one clause now: five of your mana sources make spells-only mana. It casts Dragons beautifully and it can never pay an activated ability.

The 21-point commander clock (CR 903.10a) is arithmetic worth savouring and then setting down. A 10/10 deals 20 commander damage in two connections — one point short — so it takes three clean hits, and even Thrakkus the Butcher doubling stops at 20 on a single swing. Commander damage here is a coincidence, not a plan. The kills are filed under The Kill.

The Coach's close, and it is a table read. A nine-mana commander is the best decoy in Commander: every seat prices you at turn nine while your actual game is a discounted Dragon on turn four. Let them keep the read. Cast him when the table's interaction has been spent elsewhere, shield him the turn he lands, and never mulligan a hand hunting for him. The zone already holds him, and the zone is where he earns.

captions.Hellkite Courser: **THE RENTAL CLAUSE:** his enters-trigger borrows The Ur-Dragon out of the command zone with haste for one attack — a draw per attacking Dragon plus a free permanent — and hands him back untaxed at end step.
captions.Herald's Horn: **THE DISCOUNT THAT STACKS:** {1} off every Dragon creature spell on top of eminence, plus a free look at the top of your library each upkeep. Name Dragon and stop thinking about it.

pilot_tips.text: Hold Teferi's Protection for the turn The Ur-Dragon finally lands — a nine-mana body with no shield is the most expensive way to donate a sweeper.

departments.pull_quote: The guarantee is not that you will draw him. It is that you are already being paid.

departments.headline: PAYOFF FIRST, DRAGON SECOND
departments.dek: The loop the whole table fears assembles in 6.4% of your games. Build for the payoff layer that kills in 62.2% of them, and take the loop the turn it walks in.

pilot_tips.text: Cast Dragonspeaker Shaman on turn three and spend the discount immediately — a cost reducer reaches your hand by turn six in only 33.2% of games, so the turn you have one is the turn to use it.

captions.Dragon Tempest: **THE MEDIAN KILL:** two mana, and every Dragon entering afterwards throws damage equal to your Dragon count. It pays nothing for the bodies already down, so it goes first — always.
captions.The Ur-Dragon: **THE DECOY:** mean cast turn 8.967, and 0.0% of games by turn six. Eminence does his work from the zone while three opponents budget answers for a body that mostly never arrives.
captions.Aggravated Assault: **THE CEILING, NOT THE SCHEDULE:** all three of the deck's two-card infinites route through this one enchantment, and it assembles with a mana Dragon in 3.6% of games by turn six. Play toward Dragons; take this when it arrives.

departments.pull_quote: The loop is your ceiling. Tempest plus a board is your schedule.
departments.engine_caption: THE UR-DRAGON, running. Seven stages, from 34 lands paying a five-colour bill to the one enchantment that turns a mana Dragon into unlimited combats — six of the eleven arrows carry a passing stack, and there is no fodder stage because this deck consumes nothing to make anything.
not_modelled: Stack 003's eleven damage a combat is a three-card board — Old Gnawbone is attacking alongside Savage Ventmaw. The named pair alone puts four into a forty-life seat, which is the tenth combat, not the fourth.

Stack 006 is the half that kills on schedule: seven Treasures a swing, net two a cycle, one seat dead on combat six and the second on combat twelve. It assumes nothing blocks a 7/7 flier and nobody answers the enchantment across twelve combats.
The discount this plan is built on is eminence, and no checker-passed stack has run a Dragon spell through it. The commander's own mean cast turn is 8.967, with 0.0% of games by turn six.

departments.headline: NINETY-NINE SEATS, RANKED
departments.dek: The map sorted this roster before we did: seven cities, and the largest holds a third of the deck plus most of the cards the checker has already been through. Twenty-two of your twenty-four creatures are Dragons, and your own sweepers know exactly which two are not.

roster.role: The engine room — on the record

captions.Rivaz of the Claw: **NOT A DRAGON:** he is a 3/3 Lizard Warlock, which means your own Dragonback Assault and Crux of Fate's non-Dragon mode both kill him — and his two mana is spells-only, so it will never pay Aggravated Assault.
captions.Korlessa, Scale Singer: **THE 1/4 THAT LIVES:** she is a Dragon, so Dragonback Assault's three damage bounces off and Crux of Fate leaves her standing. Deploy her early and cast Dragons off the top all game.
captions.Atsushi, the Blazing Sky: **THE WALKING BANK:** his death mints three unrestricted Treasures — exactly the mana five of your own sources are legally forbidden to provide for an activated ability.

pilot_tips.text: Empty your hand with Klauth's attack mana, but never budget it for Aggravated Assault — it pays for spells only, and an activated ability is not a spell.

departments.pull_quote: Twenty-two of your twenty-four creatures are Dragons. Learn the other two by name.
departments.constellation_caption: THE UR-DRAGON, mapped. Seven cities and fourteen neighbourhoods, re-laid-out from this deck's own cards in the function space, so a card sits beside the cards that do its job — the commander and every card named in a passing stack is labelled. Positions are LOCAL to this deck and are not atlas positions.
departments.note: Renderer draws per-card prose from manual_prose.card_roles and groups the grid by city, largest first, so the territory on the figure and the block under it share one ink. The authored roster stays in the file as the editorial reading of the same 99; the commander's entry lives in The Command Zone.

departments.headline: STOP CASTING YOUR COMMANDER
departments.dek: Sunny opens by taking the nine-drop out of the maths, then hands the Counselor the reason and asks her to check it. She takes it off him, keeps his advice, and then costs him a second argument about how fast the famous loop actually kills.
departments.pull_quote: The conclusion is sound and the reason is unearned. Those are different things.
departments.note: Sunny's hot take renders first; the panel's spine is the discount nobody has measured, so the pull quote is the Counselor's holding rather than the take. Every line in here points at a badge earned elsewhere — the department grants coach and nothing more.

departments.headline: MULLIGAN FOR FUNCTION
departments.dek: The simulation keeps 75.1% of first sevens at 0.313 mean mulligans, so your gut is usually right. Call these four out loud before you read the receipts — and know that the card the deck is really thirsty for shows up by turn six only 33.2% of the time.

hands.why: A cost reducer plus Sol Ring is the hand this deck is thirsty for: reducers arrive by turn six in just 33.2% of games, and they, not land drops, compress a 28-card shelf of five-plus-drops into something castable. Reducer plus ramp together lands by turn six 23.1% of the time — never ship one hunting for prettier Dragons.

The payoff layer pays for every Dragon that enters after it and nothing for the ones already down, so it wants to be first. A payoff is drawn by turn six in 62.2% of games; this hand has one on turn two, which is how you beat that number instead of matching it.

hands.verdict: KEEP — the loud card, held quietly
hands.why: Assault in an opener is a hold, not a keep-reason — on turn three it only announces you. The keep is the ramp, the engine half and Atsushi, whose death mints three unrestricted Treasures. Those Treasures, not your Dragon-restricted sources, are what pays {3}{R}{R} later.

Two lands, five cards at mana value five or more, and no bridge between them. Mean available mana on turn six is 4.937 and the land drop there is 49.7% — this hand starts working around turn eight and the game will not wait for it.

pilot_tips.text: Keep almost any seven holding Urza's Incubator — with eminence it takes {3} off every Dragon, and the ledger says another reducer is not coming soon.

departments.pull_quote: Never mulligan toward the commander. The zone already holds him.

departments.headline: COMMIT BEFORE YOU PEEK
departments.dek: Two real boards from this exact 99: a castable commander staring into five untapped control lands, and a Tiamat pile you have to design into telegraphed sweeper mana. Decide out loud first — the Coach shows his hand after you show yours.
departments.pull_quote: A good read costs nothing. A bad commit costs the game.
departments.note: Render decisions 001 then 002. Recommendations stay below the branches per STYLEv3 §5.1 — no caption, callout or dek may telegraph either answer.

departments.headline: SIX VERDICTS, ONE PAYROLL
departments.dek: Two true infinites, a d20 burst, a doubling audit, a sweeper turned into an execution, and a famous cheat denied in court. Every line here survived the adversarial checker — including the ones whose limits are smaller than the internet thinks.

callouts.title: THE SWING
callouts.text: Old Gnawbone connects for 7 in the air. Treasures equal to the combat damage dealt to players — seven tokens hit the battlefield (stack 006).

callouts.title: THE PAYMENT
callouts.text: Five of those Treasures pay Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R}. Untap your creatures, take another combat phase, and note that your five lands were never touched.

callouts.title: THE MARGIN
callouts.text: Seven in, five out: net +2 Treasures a cycle. The moment nothing on the board can block a 7/7 flier, the loop has no upper bound.

callouts.title: THE EXECUTIONS
callouts.text: Opponents die in sequence, not together — the 40-life seat on combat 6, the 38-life seat on combat 12 of the verified game.

callouts.title: THE ACCOUNTING
callouts.text: You finish holding exactly 22 Treasures, not 29: the game ends by state-based action before Gnawbone's twelfth trigger ever resolves.

captions.Savage Ventmaw: **THE SELF-FUNDING LOOP:** the attack trigger's {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G} pays the reactivation with {R} to spare, and it fires on declaration, before blockers matter (stack 003).
captions.Sneak Attack: **THE REFUTATION:** {R} cheats any Dragon in the 99 into play, and it cannot touch The Ur-Dragon — the command zone is not your hand (stack 005). Drakuseth still deals all 17 before the end-step sacrifice.
captions.Wrathful Red Dragon: **THE HONEST LIMIT:** three Dragons dealt 13 sends 39 at one opponent, which kills a seat at 32 and cannot also reach one at 40. Destroy-all wraths feed him nothing (stack 004).

pilot_tips.text: Guard Aggravated Assault like the win condition it is — all three infinites route through it, no second extra-combat effect is sleeved, and of your tutors only Enlightened Tutor can find an enchantment at all.

departments.pull_quote: The database alleges. The checker adjudicates.
departments.note: Feature order: 006 (the cover line, walked in the callout-steps), 003, 001, 002, 004, 005. Case pointers A-001 through A-006 are renderer-standing. Two of the deck's three contained two-card infinites are the ones on this docket; the Cavern-Hoard Dragon line is named as unverified everywhere it appears.

departments.headline: THE SLOWEST DECK IN THE ROOM
departments.dek: Five-colour Dragons reads as battlecruiser, and your first four turns confirm the story — 1.463 bodies by turn six is nobody's emergency. Keep it that way, because your real tells get answered on sight and you cannot re-buy either of them.

enemy.headline: FIVE FIGHTS, NAMED OUTS
enemy.dek: Sweepers, taxes, aggro, faster combo and the graveyard. Four of them you beat with cards that are actually sleeved in this 99 — and the fifth is the one this deck cannot answer at all, so read that box twice.

tutors.headline: FOUR WISHES, ONE ENCHANTMENT
tutors.dek: Four tutors get a real decision here, thirteen wishes between them, and three of the four are not shopping for a Dragon at all. A wish is also an announcement — shop the turn before you need the card, never two.

threats.read: Your board is thin by design — 1.463 mean bodies at turn six — so a wave costs you less than it costs the token seat, and your rebuild is enchantment-shaped: Aggravated Assault, Sneak Attack, Dragon Tempest and Garruk's Uprising all sit under a creature wrath untouched. With Wrathful Red Dragon down, a damage sweeper is their mistake (stack 004). Destroy-all and exile-all effects still trade clean, so keep one shield for the board that actually wins.

Taxes land hardest on a 28-card shelf of five-plus-drops sitting on 4.937 mean mana at turn six. Two things break the maths back: eminence discounts every Dragon spell from a zone permanent-hate cannot reach, and Treasure bursts pay a whole tax in one lump. Name the piece that beats you — an untap denier, or anything taxing an activated ability — because your exit is an activated ability.

You are the control seat: roughly 120 combined life sits behind three defences, and 20 of your creatures fly with toughness four or better, so a ground board never arrives. Read Crux of Fate before you call it one-sided — the non-Dragon mode kills Dragonspeaker Shaman and Rivaz of the Claw, your only two non-Dragon creatures, and it is {3}{B}{B} on the colour that lands on curve 44.6% of the time.

Held answers rot, and the last profitable moment is their win attempt — spend nothing before it. You also race credibly rather than purely reacting: all three of your two-card lines need no mana beyond the pieces themselves. Price Deflecting Swat and Flawless Maneuver at three mana each, since their free clause wants a commander on the battlefield and yours mostly is not.

This is the fun one, and the fun is that you lose it on paper: nothing in the 99 touches an opposing graveyard. There is no answer to the yard, so there is only the stack and the clock. Counter the enabler rather than the body, because once the reanimated thing resolves you have one Chaos Warp and a prayer. When their hate points at you instead, shrug — Patriarch's Bidding and Haven of the Spirit Dragon are bonuses, not the spine.

callouts.title: WINDOW ONE
callouts.text: You flip to archenemy the turn Aggravated Assault is live with Old Gnawbone or Savage Ventmaw connecting — funding on the board, protection in hand. The shield is there by turn six in 66.0% of games. Choose the turn; never drift into it.

callouts.title: WINDOW TWO
callouts.text: With Wrathful Red Dragon on the battlefield, welcome the damage sweeper: 39 redirected at one face (stack 004). Say the number out loud before their turn — naming the seat it kills usually keeps the wrath in their hand, which most nights is worth more than the kill.

callouts.title: THE HONEST DISCLOSURE
callouts.text: When someone asks whether you are the combo deck, tell the truth: the loop assembles in 6.4% of games. You are the Dragon deck that occasionally draws a better ending, and saying so buys you turns that lying never would.

captions.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: **THE HEAT MAGNET:** she doubles every nontoken Dragon after her from behind ward {2}, and everyone at the table has watched that happen to someone. Expect her to eat the removal your engine wanted.
captions.Dragonlord Dromoka: **THE QUIET COMMIT:** opponents cannot cast spells during your turn. Sequence her first on the pivot turn and everything after her resolves in peace.

pilot_tips.text: Save Deflecting Swat for the removal aimed at Aggravated Assault mid-combo — and price it at three mana, because the commander is rarely on the battlefield to make it free.
Count your two non-Dragons before you cast Crux of Fate — the non-Dragon mode kills Dragonspeaker Shaman and Rivaz of the Claw, so fire it after the Shaman has already bought you a discount.

Cast Enlightened Tutor the turn before you need the card, never the turn you do — it puts the card on top of your library, and the reveal announces Aggravated Assault to three opponents who now have a turn to answer it.

departments.pull_quote: Stay boring until the turn you aren't.
departments.note: One act, one opener: the table read leads, the five threat boxes and the matchup prose sit under the first subhead, the tutor guide under the second. Furniture carried forward whole — three callouts, two captions, three PILOT TIPs, one per turn of the argument. Fetch Quests' pull quote survives inside the tutors dek, since a department may print only one.

departments.headline: IT MISSES TURNS, NOT COLOURS
departments.dek: Red carries 46.5% of the pip load on 28.6% of the sources, and black finishes on curve just 26.1% of the time from lands alone. But the number that actually binds is plainer: 34 lands against the 36 to 38 the template asks for, and a land drop that falls to 49.7% by turn six.

captions.The World Tree: **THE SECOND LANTERN:** at six lands every land you control taps for any colour, and five separate colour shortfalls collapse into one solved number.
captions.Chromatic Lantern: **FIXING BEFORE YOU NEED IT:** it turns every land into an any-colour source, which is worth far more than the one mana it makes. Play it the turn before the double-pip spell, never on the turn you already need it.

pilot_tips.text: Fetch the Swamp with Fabled Passage the turn before Patriarch's Bidding or Crux of Fate — black is the thinnest column on the board, and its eight pips arrive in double-black lumps.

departments.pull_quote: This base rarely misses a colour. It misses turns.

departments.headline: SIX POINT FOUR, AND SIXTY-TWO POINT TWO
departments.dek: Aggravated Assault plus a mana Dragon assembles in 6.4% of ten thousand seeded runs, at a mean of turn 5.442. A Dragon payoff is in hand by turn six in 62.2%, and the deck lives in that gap.

callouts.title: EARLY MONEY
callouts.text: Ramp or fixing is drawn by turn six in 71.6% of games at a mean arrival of turn 2.588. The first act funds itself.

callouts.title: THE RARE FIXER
callouts.text: A cost reducer shows by turn six in only 33.2% of games — and the model does not simulate the discount at all, so when you hold one, build the turn around it.

callouts.title: THE FADE
callouts.text: The land drop holds at 88.3% on turn three, then falls to 60.3% on five and 49.7% on six, with mean mana at 4.937. You miss a land as often as you hit one on exactly the turns the plan has to deploy.

callouts.title: THE CEILING
callouts.text: The infinite-combat component assembles in 6.4% of games, 3.6% by turn six. It is measured, it is certified twice over, and it is not a plan you can wait for.

captions.Urza's Incubator: **OFF THE BOOKS:** cost reducers go unmodelled, so mean cast turn 8.967 is the floor of the commander problem rather than your ceiling.
captions.Old Gnawbone: **ALSO OFF THE BOOKS:** the simulation mints no Treasures, so the deck's richest income line is invisible to every number on this page.

pilot_tips.text: Never count Mox Jasper as mana in an opening hand — it only taps while you control a Dragon, so it is a blank until the board shows up.

departments.pull_quote: The commander is an event. The loop is a ceiling. The Dragons are the schedule.

departments.headline: SIX BUY MANA, THREE BUY INSURANCE
departments.dek: Ten cards worth knowing about, and the split tells the story: six buy mana or discount because 34 lands is what binds this deck, three buy a second card name for an extra-combat plan resting on one enchantment, and the tenth answers the graveyard — the only class nothing in the 99 touches.

callouts.title: THE STANDING RULE
callouts.text: Every combo line these picks open is a candidate, not a fact — each one reads 'needs a stack scenario'. And no pick moves the computed bracket floor off 4, because three two-card infinites already paid for it.

callouts.title: THE FAMILY THAT MISSED
callouts.text: The Reaver Cleaver opens the most-played Aggravated Assault line in the database, and Sword of Feast and Famine and Bear Umbra both untap lands to fund the next activation. None of them makes Assault replaceable, which is the actual hole. Helm of the Host skips Assault entirely and then costs 4 to cast plus 5 to equip against 4.937 mean mana at turn six — priced out before its rules question is even asked.

pilot_tips.text: If Three Visits earns a sleeve, Skyshroud Claim is the card it replaces — the obsolescence trace reads 0.9936 similarity at two less mana value, and Nature's Lore and Farseek already do the same job here.

departments.pull_quote: When one enchantment carries three infinites, a second card name is the cheapest insurance on the board.

departments.headline: SIX CASES, VERBATIM
departments.dek: Every citation quoted in full, every verdict stamped after an adversarial second read. Case A-005 alone is worth the visit: the famous cheat, denied, with the rule that denies it.
departments.note: Cases A-001 through A-006 render from the checker-passed stacks with citations untouched. A-006 backs the cover line; A-005 carries the CR 903.6 refutation the teases sell; A-003 and A-006 are the two certified halves of the extra-combat plan.

departments.headline: SEVENTY-SIX HANDS, NO OWNER
departments.dek: Nobody owns this deck: 76 artists across 95 cards, and the largest single hand is four. The ledger calls that breadth rather than indecision — and it counts every hand per card, never per copy.

featured.note:
The lead hand here is four cards out of 95, which is not a standout and we are not going to pretend otherwise. What makes Adam Paquette the right seat anyway is what those four are: Blood Crypt, Cinder Glade, Steam Vents and Dragon's Hoard — three duals and the artifact that fixes and draws. In an issue whose binding constraint is mana, the largest portfolio in the deck is entirely infrastructure. He painted the bills.

Read the counts for exactly what they are. They are per card, never per copy: the four Mountains share one Jonas De Ro painting and count once, and the three Forests count once for Tomáš Honz. Counting copies would hand the top of this list to two basic-land arts and call it authorship.

The breadth is structural. The 95 cards arrive from 41 different products, the biggest cluster is eight cards from Tarkir: Dragonstorm Commander spread across eight different painters, and no collector-number run suggests a product bought whole and dropped in. Jaime Jones has three, including the commander portrait the whole table prices. Nobody has five. This deck was assembled one Dragon at a time, and the ledger shows it: zero borderless, exactly one foil, and 76 hands on 95 cards.

also_worth_noting.note: Three, and one of them is the face of the franchise: The Ur-Dragon, plus Dragonlord Kolaghan's haste anthem and the Temur Ascendancy that turns your board into cards.
Three, all load-bearing: Drakuseth, Maw of Flames — the Dragon case A-005 cheats into play — with Urza's Incubator and Rootbound Crag.
Three, including the deck's most misread card: Rivaz of the Claw, a Lizard Warlock among 22 Dragons, beside Terror of the Peaks and Heroic Intervention.
Two, and both make mana with a catch — Goldspan Dragon's Treasures pay for anything, Klauth's attack mana pays for spells only.

captions.The Ur-Dragon: **THE FACE:** Jaime Jones' commander portrait — the one card three opponents price all game, painted at hero scale for a body that lands in 13.7% of ten-turn games.

departments.pull_quote: Breadth all the way down — one Dragon at a time.

departments.note: next_issue reads TO BE ANNOUNCED, so the teaser stays the standing series line rather than a named deck. The colophon carries decklist sha edc6644d0683 and the rules version automatically.

rhythm_notes: Act I meets the deck in order of what a player would tell you: the Counselor's Command Zone instruction, then Sunny's narrative plan, then the roster's low-intensity browse. Act II climbs — the hand drill, the two participation spreads of What's Your Play, and The Kill as the act's peak, where the 006 payroll is walked step by step and reads as narrative despite carrying the densest rules content in the issue. Act III is three straight Coach sections by design: reflection at the table, the reference block of Know Your Enemy between two instruction spreads, and Fetch Quests to exit. Act IV is Ledger's three, and it is the one place two dense analysis modes meet: the renderer's declared full-bleed breather sits between Sources Say and By the Numbers, and The Short List's imagination mode cools the act out. Act V parks Judge's Desk's opt-in density behind Act IV rather than behind The Kill, exhales through Featured Artist, and exits on the Back Page. Pull quotes act as micro-breathers on the eight longest sections; the only section without one is Know Your Enemy, where five threat boxes already break the page. AMENDED: Act III's three Coach departments (Table Manners, Know Your Enemy, Fetch Quests) have since merged into the single At the Table, which carries all three arguments under written subheads — so any buffering described above between those three is now internal to one department, and the Editor's Letter and the Pilot's Log have joined Act I with the panel running last, behind The 99.
gaps: Cavern-Hoard Dragon + Aggravated Assault is the one contained two-card infinite with no stack. Its Treasures count the DEFENDING player's artifacts, so the scenario would bound the line rather than bless it — until then every section names it as unverified.

Two frame-flagged scenarios worth buying next: Sneak Attack at instant speed cheating Wrathful Red Dragon in under a sweeper (it would extend verified case A-004), and Miirym plus Sneak Attack — does the token copy survive the end-step sacrifice? A yes changes the rate of the whole velocity plan.

The three cost reducers versus the commander is an unsettled rules question with a planning consequence: Urza's Incubator and Herald's Horn reduce creature spells of a chosen type, Dragonspeaker Shaman reduces Dragon spells, and eminence says 'other'. Whether all three stack on a nine-drop Dragon Avatar deserves a scenario, since the goldfish measures a 'turn-5-Ur-Dragon hand' at 33.9% without it.

Short List scenarios in priority order, from considering.json: Old Gnawbone + Hellkite Charger (the combo record itself lists mana_value_needed 7, so the question is whether one connection funds the next activation), then Najeela, the Blade-Blossom + Old Gnawbone (whether Treasure-funded {W}{U}{B}{R}{G} sustains across combats with black at 16 sources).

Strategy DB holes this issue felt directly: extra-combat chaining as a school of its own, kill-order sequencing when a verified line kills opponents in sequence (case A-006 does), cheat-into-play economics, typal payoff density, and a vocabulary for five-colour bases where 16 tapped lands and 5 unconditional ones are very different facts.
